## AbletonOSC Overview

AbletonOSC is a MIDI remote script that provides an Open Sound Control (OSC) interface to control Ableton Live. The project's aim is to expose the entire Live Object Model API, providing comprehensive control over Live's control interfaces using the same naming structure and object hierarchy as LOM.

## Requirements and Installation

AbletonOSC requires Ableton Live 11 or above. To install the script, download a zip of the repository, unzip its contents, and rename AbletonOSC-master to AbletonOSC, then install it by copying the AbletonOSC folder to the Remote Scripts directory.

## Communication Details

AbletonOSC listens for OSC messages on port 11000, and sends replies on port 11001. Replies will be sent to the same IP as the originating message.

## Python Implementation

In AbletonOSC, Open Sound Control parsing and generation is achieved with the python-osc library, a native Python implementation of the OSC 1.0 specification. You can use Python libraries like `pythonosc` to send OSC commands to control Ableton Live programmatically.

## Usage Example

Included with the framework is a command-line console utility run-console.py, which can be used as a quick and easy way to send OSC queries to AbletonOSC.

Here's what exists across two categories: **offline file parsing** (read/write .als projects) and **live control** (interact with a running Ableton instance).

---

## Offline: .als File Parsing

Ableton .als files are gzipped XML, so they're very parseable. Key libraries:

| Tool | Language | Capabilities |
|---|---|---|
| [pyableton](https://github.com/maranedah/pyableton) | Python | Parse .als files, extract track/clip/device info. On PyPI. |
| [loive](https://github.com/naglalakk/loive) | Python | List devices, plugins, print project summaries |
| [alsd](https://github.com/andrewcb/alsd) | Python | Standalone .als reader, no Live dependency |
| [walmik/ableton](https://github.com/walmik/ableton) | Node.js | .als parser |
| [MusicTech Lab Analyser](https://www.musictechlab.io/blog/software-development/extracting-data-from-ableton-als-asd-files) | Python | Parses both .als and .asd (sample metadata) files |

Since .als is just gzip + XML, you can also roll your own with `gzip` + `xml.etree` in Python. The XML contains the full project state: tracks, clips, MIDI notes, automation, device chains, mixer settings, tempo, etc.

---

## Live Control: MCP Servers & OSC

This is where the agent story gets interesting — multiple MCP servers already exist:

| Tool | Approach | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [jpoindexter/ableton-mcp](https://github.com/jpoindexter/ableton-mcp) | MCP + REST + Max4Live | **200+ tools**, near-complete Live Object Model coverage. Works with Claude, Ollama, OpenAI, Groq. The most mature option. |
| [ahujasid/ableton-mcp](https://github.com/ahujasid/ableton-mcp) | MCP | Simpler variant, Claude Desktop focused |
| [ableton-mcp-extended](https://github.com/uisato/ableton-mcp-extended) | MCP | Extended feature set |
| [FabianTinkl/AbletonMCP](https://github.com/FabianTinkl/AbletonMCP) | MCP | MIDI composition, transport, parameter manipulation |
| [AbletonOSC](https://github.com/ideoforms/AbletonOSC) | OSC (port 11000/11001) | Max4Live remote script exposing the full Live Object Model via OSC. The foundation most MCP servers build on. |
| [AbletonPython](https://github.com/nrox/AbletonPython) | Python direct | Control Live 11 via Python |

---

## AI-Specific Tools

- [Magenta Studio](https://www.ableton.com/en/blog/magenta-studio-free-ai-tools-ableton-live/) — Google's free Max4Live devices for ML-based generation (continuation, interpolation, drumming)
- [MIDI Agent](https://www.midiagent.com/ai-midi-generator-for-ableton-live) — AI MIDI generation VST/AU plugin
- [Melosurf](https://www.musicradar.com/music-tech/is-this-the-future-of-the-daw-melosurf-is-a-voice-controlled-ai-assistant-that-lets-you-talk-to-ableton-live) — Voice-controlled AI assistant for Live

---

## What This Means for Your Pipeline

For an agent that can **read, understand, write, and give feedback** on your projects, there are two viable architectures:

1. **Offline analysis** (pyableton or raw gzip+XML parsing) — Agent reads .als files directly, analyzes arrangement structure, mix decisions, MIDI content, device chains, and gives feedback without Ableton running. This is the simpler path and fits a pipeline well.

2. **Live MCP bridge** (jpoindexter/ableton-mcp) — Agent connects to a running Ableton instance, can read state AND write changes back (create tracks, add MIDI clips, adjust parameters). More powerful but requires Ableton to be open.

The **jpoindexter/ableton-mcp** server is the most complete existing solution — 200+ tools, already speaks MCP, works with Claude. Want me to dig deeper into any of these, or start sketching out how one of these would integrate with your pipeline?

### 1. pyableton (offline .als parsing)

```
Context: I'm building an AI agent pipeline that can read, understand, write, and give feedback on Ableton Live music production projects. I need a deep-dive research report on a specific tool in this ecosystem. The findings will be used to create skill files and enrich domain models for agents operating in my workspace.

Deep-dive: pyableton (https://github.com/maranedah/pyableton, https://pypi.org/project/pyableton/)

Research the following and produce a structured report:

1. **Capabilities & Coverage**
   - What parts of the .als XML schema does it actually parse? (tracks, clips, MIDI notes, audio refs, devices, automation, mixer, tempo, time signature, markers, scenes, etc.)
   - Can it WRITE .als files or is it read-only?
   - Does it handle all Ableton versions or only specific ones?

2. **API Surface**
   - Key classes and methods. What does the object model look like?
   - Code examples of common operations (load project, iterate tracks, read MIDI clips, read device chains)
   - What data structures does it return? (dicts, dataclasses, custom objects?)

3. **Gaps & Limitations**
   - What parts of .als files does it NOT parse?
   - Known issues or stale maintenance (check last commit, open issues, PR activity)
   - Does it handle edge cases like frozen tracks, grouped tracks, Max4Live devices, nested racks?

4. **Integration Fitness**
   - How easy would it be to wrap this as an MCP tool or agent skill?
   - Could an agent use this to give meaningful feedback on arrangement structure, mix balance, sound design choices, MIDI writing quality?
   - What would an agent NOT be able to assess using this alone?

5. **Alternatives Comparison**
   - How does it compare to raw gzip+xml.etree parsing? What value does the library add over DIY?
   - Compare briefly to loive and alsd — is pyableton the best choice for offline parsing?

Produce the report in markdown with clear sections. Include code snippets where they illuminate the API. Flag anything that's uncertain vs confirmed from source code.
```

### 2. AbletonOSC (OSC foundation layer)

```
Context: I'm building an AI agent pipeline that can read, understand, write, and give feedback on Ableton Live music production projects. I need a deep-dive research report on a specific tool in this ecosystem. The findings will be used to create skill files and enrich domain models for agents operating in my workspace.

Deep-dive: AbletonOSC (https://github.com/ideoforms/AbletonOSC)

This is the Max4Live remote script that exposes the Ableton Live Object Model via OSC. Many MCP servers build on top of it. Research the following:

1. **Protocol & Architecture**
   - How does the OSC message routing work? (ports 11000/11001, message format, reply structure)
   - What is the full namespace of OSC addresses it exposes? Categorize by domain (transport, tracks, clips, devices, mixer, scenes, arrangement, etc.)
   - Is it request/response only, or does it support subscriptions/listeners for state changes?

2. **Live Object Model Coverage**
   - How much of Ableton's LOM does it actually expose?
   - Can it read AND write? (e.g., can you create clips, add MIDI notes, change device parameters, not just query them?)
   - What operations are missing compared to what the full LOM supports?

3. **Installation & Requirements**
   - Ableton version requirements (Live 11+? Live 12?)
   - Max4Live dependency — does it need Suite or just Standard+M4L?
   - Any OS-specific gotchas?

4. **Performance & Reliability**
   - Latency characteristics for OSC round-trips
   - Can it handle rapid-fire queries (e.g., agent dumping full project state)?
   - Known stability issues under heavy use?

5. **Integration Fitness**
   - This is the transport layer most MCP servers use. What are the implications of building directly on AbletonOSC vs using an MCP wrapper?
   - Could a Python agent use python-osc to talk to this directly?
   - What would a "read full project state" operation look like over OSC vs parsing .als offline?

6. **Ecosystem Role**
   - Which MCP servers depend on this? How do they extend it?
   - Is this the canonical/best-maintained OSC interface, or are there competitors?

Produce the report in markdown. Include the OSC address namespace organized by category if possible. Flag the read-vs-write capability for each category.
```

### 3. jpoindexter/ableton-mcp (most mature MCP server)

```
Context: I'm building an AI agent pipeline that can read, understand, write, and give feedback on Ableton Live music production projects. I need a deep-dive research report on a specific tool in this ecosystem. The findings will be used to create skill files and enrich domain models for agents operating in my workspace.

Deep-dive: jpoindexter/ableton-mcp (https://github.com/jpoindexter/ableton-mcp)

This claims 200+ tools and near-complete LOM coverage. I need to know if it lives up to that. Research the following:

1. **Tool Inventory**
   - List or categorize ALL exposed MCP tools. Group by domain: transport, tracks, clips, MIDI, audio, devices, mixer, scenes, arrangement, browser, etc.
   - For each category: what can you READ vs WRITE vs EXECUTE?
   - Are there any "AI-specific" tools (e.g., generate MIDI, suggest arrangement) or is it purely a control surface?

2. **Architecture**
   - How does it work? (MCP server → ? → AbletonOSC → Max4Live → Live?)
   - Does it bundle its own Max4Live device or depend on AbletonOSC?
   - REST API mode — how does that work? Can it run headless?
   - What's the Max4Live device doing specifically?

3. **MCP Protocol Compliance**
   - Does it implement MCP properly? (tool definitions, input schemas, error handling)
   - Are the tool definitions well-typed with good descriptions, or rough/undocumented?
   - Does it support resources or prompts (MCP concepts beyond tools)?

4. **Agent Workflow Fitness**
   - Can an agent use this to: analyze a project's structure? give feedback on mixing? write MIDI? suggest arrangement changes? compare two versions?
   - What's the typical latency for a "dump full project state" operation?
   - Are there batch operations or does every query need its own tool call?

5. **Maturity & Maintenance**
   - Last commit, release cadence, open issues, contributor count
   - Is it production-quality or experimental?
   - Any security considerations (it exposes a REST API)?

6. **Setup Complexity**
   - What's the full installation path? (Max4Live device + Python server + MCP config?)
   - Does it work with Claude Code / Claude Desktop out of the box?

Produce the report in markdown. The tool inventory section is the most important — be as comprehensive as possible. Include example MCP tool call JSON if available.
```

### 4. ahujasid/ableton-mcp (simpler MCP variant)

```
Context: I'm building an AI agent pipeline that can read, understand, write, and give feedback on Ableton Live music production projects. I need a deep-dive research report on a specific tool in this ecosystem. The findings will be used to create skill files and enrich domain models for agents operating in my workspace.

Deep-dive: ahujasid/ableton-mcp (https://github.com/ahujasid/ableton-mcp)

This appears to be a simpler/earlier MCP server for Ableton. I need to understand what it offers and how it compares to jpoindexter's version. Research the following:

1. **Tool Inventory**
   - What MCP tools does it expose? List them all with brief descriptions.
   - Categorize by: transport, tracks, clips, MIDI, devices, mixer, scenes.
   - Read vs write capabilities for each.

2. **Architecture**
   - How does it connect to Ableton? (AbletonOSC? Custom remote script? Direct API?)
   - What dependencies does it require?
   - How does it differ architecturally from jpoindexter/ableton-mcp?

3. **Differentiation**
   - What does this do that jpoindexter's version doesn't (if anything)?
   - What does it lack compared to jpoindexter's version?
   - Is this a fork, predecessor, or independent implementation?
   - Is there a reason to use this over jpoindexter's version?

4. **Maturity**
   - Maintenance status (last commit, issues, stars, forks)
   - Documentation quality
   - Is this actively developed or abandoned?

5. **Agent Fitness**
   - Is the tool set sufficient for an agent to give meaningful feedback on a project?
   - Any unique capabilities that would complement other tools?

Produce a concise markdown report. Focus on what's unique or different about this compared to the jpoindexter version — don't spend time documenting overlap.
```

### 5. uisato/ableton-mcp-extended

```
Context: I'm building an AI agent pipeline that can read, understand, write, and give feedback on Ableton Live music production projects. I need a deep-dive research report on a specific tool in this ecosystem. The findings will be used to create skill files and enrich domain models for agents operating in my workspace.

Deep-dive: uisato/ableton-mcp-extended (https://github.com/uisato/ableton-mcp-extended)

The name implies this extends a base ableton-mcp. I need to know what the extensions are and whether they add meaningful capability. Research the following:

1. **What's Extended?**
   - What base does this fork/extend? (ahujasid's? jpoindexter's? independent?)

2. **Tool Inventory**

3. **Architecture Differences**

4. **Unique Value**

   - Any tools related to analysis, mixing feedback, arrangement review?

5. **Maturity & Maintenance**
   - Activity level, documentation, known issues.
   - Is this actively maintained or a one-off fork?

Produce a concise markdown report focused on the DELTA — what this adds beyond the base implementation. If the extensions are trivial, say so directly.
```

### 6. FabianTinkl/AbletonMCP (MIDI composition focus)

```
Context: I'm building an AI agent pipeline that can read, understand, write, and give feedback on Ableton Live music production projects. I need a deep-dive research report on a specific tool in this ecosystem. The findings will be used to create skill files and enrich domain models for agents operating in my workspace.

Deep-dive: FabianTinkl/AbletonMCP (https://github.com/FabianTinkl/AbletonMCP)

This variant emphasizes MIDI composition, transport control, and parameter manipulation. Research the following:

   - All MCP tools, categorized by domain.

3. **Architecture**
   - How does it connect to Ableton? What's the stack?

4. **Parameter Manipulation**
   - How deep is device parameter control? (can you read/write specific knob values on specific devices?)
   - Can it navigate into instrument/effect racks, drum racks, nested chains?
   - Can it read current parameter values for analysis purposes?

5. **Agent Fitness for Feedback**
   - Could an agent use this to analyze MIDI content quality? (note density, velocity dynamics, chord voicings, rhythmic patterns)
   - Could it read device parameter states to assess sound design choices?
   - What's missing for a "production feedback" use case?

6. **Maturity**
   - Maintenance status, documentation quality, known issues.
   - How does it compare in completeness to jpoindexter's version?

Produce the report in markdown. The MIDI composition section is the highest priority — that's the potential differentiator. Include code/JSON examples of MIDI tool calls if available.
```

---

Each prompt should produce a standalone research doc. When they come back, you'll be able to compare them side-by-side and distill the useful bits into skill files and domain knowledge for your agents.

{'role': 'user', 'content': [{'tool_use_id': 'toolu_013akhTTCWUpSE9KPY1kFGA1', 'type': 'tool_result', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Now I'll compile a comprehensive summary based on all the documents I've read:

## Summary of ALS Reader Documentation

### 1. One-Line Summaries of Each Document

| File | Coverage |
|------|----------|
| **ableton-mcp-agent-fitness.md** | Evaluates how well the MCP server supports agent workflows (reads: good; writes: partial; audio analysis: none) |
| **ableton-mcp-extended.md** | Analyzes uisato's extended MCP fork which adds 30 commands at Remote Script level but exposes only 1 new MCP tool |
| **ableton-mcp-overview.md** | JPoindexter's comprehensive MCP fork (128 tools, 2.0.0) across 19 domains vs base ahujasid version (16 tools) |
| **ableton-mcp-tool-inventory.md** | Complete catalog of all 128 MCP tools with R/W/X status and parameter details |
| **abletonosc-coverage-gaps.md** | Maps AbletonOSC's ~40-50% LOM coverage against critical gaps (master track, returns, racks, browser, automation) |
| **abletonosc-ecosystem.md** | Reviews MCP projects built on AbletonOSC, hybrid approaches, and OSC vs MCP trade-offs |
| **abletonosc-namespace.md** | Complete OSC address namespace documentation (song, track, clip, device, scene, view, MIDI map) |
| **abletonosc-protocol.md** | Architecture, UDP ports 11000/11001, tick-based processing (10 Hz), listener subscription mechanism |
| **ahujasid-ableton-mcp.md** | Original MCP project with only 16 tools; jpoindexter is the proper superset (not ahujasid) |
| **alternatives-comparison.md** | Compares 4 ALS parsers; recommends custom gzip+xml.etree over pyableton |
| **design-brief.md** | Custom ALS parser architecture: 5-tier data extraction (core→arrangement→mix→sound→automation), dataclass models, JSON output |
| **pyableton-research.md** | Analysis of pyableton (v0.0.15): covers ~20% of schema, crashes on real files, many commented-out features, stale since 2024-02 |

---

### 2. Key Architectural Conclusions Across All Docs

#### **Tools Maturity Assessment**

**Mature & Production-Ready:**
- **ahujasid/ableton-mcp** (2,300+ stars): Original MCP, stable but limited (16 tools, write-only for MIDI)
- **jpoindexter/ableton-mcp** (newer, 128 tools): Experimental (7 stars, 7 weeks old, zero community interaction) but substantially more capable. Covers read/write for MIDI, devices, mixer, scenes, arrangement, automation
- **AbletonOSC** (707 stars): Mature beta. Remote Script + UDP. 10 Hz tick rate, ~100-200ms latency. Known multi-client bug and listener index drift issues

**Low-Maturity / Reference Only:**
- **uisato/ableton-mcp-extended** (139 stars): 30 remote script commands but only 1 new MCP tool exposed; implementation-complete but wiring gap
- **Simon-Kansara/ableton-live-mcp-server** (369 stars): Only significant MCP actually using AbletonOSC as transport; futures-based async with 5s timeout

#### **Read vs Read-Write Capabilities**

| Tool | Read | Write | Execute | Notes |
|------|------|-------|---------|-------|
| **ahujasid/MCP (16 tools)** | Good (session/track structure) | Partial (MIDI, devices, no read-back) | Poor (transport, playback only) | Cannot read what you write |
| **jpoindexter/MCP (128 tools)** | Excellent (notes, devices, mixer, routing, automation) | Excellent (clips, notes, devices, mixer, scenes) | Good (transport, scenes, clips) | Full r/w for most domains |
| **AbletonOSC (100+ addresses)** | Good (song, track, clips, devices, automation) | Excellent (all properties) | Excellent (all methods) | Single-client only; multi-client breaks |
| **pyableton (ALS parser)** | Poor (~20% of schema) | None (read-only) | N/A | Crashes on real files; many stubs |

#### **Critical Gaps Across All Tools**

1. **Audio Content:** No tool can export/analyze audio waveforms, spectral content, or loudness. This is the fundamental blocker for "does it sound good?" feedback.
2. **No Batch Operations:** All tools require sequential queries. Full project snapshot = 200+ tool calls (ahujasid/jpoindexter).
3. **Arrangement View Clips:** ahujasid cannot read/write arrangement timeline; jpoindexter improves this but AbletonOSC only has batch name/length queries.
4. **Master & Return Tracks:** AbletonOSC has high-priority issues (#47, #189) for these. ahujasid doesn't expose them at all.
5. **Rack Traversal:** Cannot navigate into Instrument/Effect Racks — all tools see only top-level device list.
6. **Browser Loading:** Only ahujasid/jpoindexter expose browser queries; AbletonOSC has #66, #183 gaps.
7. **Multi-Client Support:** AbletonOSC has confirmed single-client-only bug (#73). Custom Remote Scripts (ahujasid/jpoindexter) avoid this.

#### **Transport & Latency Profile**

- **AbletonOSC:** 10 Hz tick rate → ~100-200ms round-trip, fire-and-forget for writes
- **ahujasid/jpoindexter (TCP/JSON):** 5-50ms simple reads, 50-200ms writes, 1-5s full project dump

Here's a prompt for a fresh agent to synthesize the research and build the tool:

```
You are building a custom Ableton Live Set (.als) parser for an AI agent pipeline. The goal: let agents read, understand, write feedback on, and eventually write to Ableton music production projects — without Ableton running.

## Context

Research has already been completed and lives at:
  /Users/brach/Documents/THE_FACTORY/enable/als-reader/docs/

Read ALL files in that directory before starting. The key findings are:

- .als files are gzipped XML containing the full project state
- pyableton (the main existing library) covers ~20% of the schema and crashes on real files — not viable
- The recommended path is a custom parser using only Python gzip + xml.etree.ElementTree (zero external deps)
- design-brief.md contains the intended architecture and 5-tier extraction priority
- The MCP research docs provide context on what data is useful for agent feedback (structure, arrangement, mix, sound design, automation)

## Your Task

Build the custom ALS parser defined in design-brief.md. Follow its architecture:

```
als_reader/
├── parser.py          # gzip decompress + ET parse
├── models.py          # Dataclasses for domain objects
├── extractors/        # Modular extractors (tracks, clips, MIDI, mixer, devices, automation, transport, scenes)
└── serialize.py       # to_json() for LLM consumption
```

### Build sequence:

1. **Read all research docs** in /enable/als-reader/docs/ — especially design-brief.md, pyableton-research.md, and alternatives-comparison.md. Absorb the schema knowledge and design decisions.

2. **Find a real .als file** to work with. Check for any .als files in the workspace. If none exist, create a minimal valid .als test fixture (gzipped XML matching Ableton's schema) for development. Having a real file to parse against is critical.

3. **Implement Tier 1 (Core) first:**
   - gzip decompression + XML parse
   - Version detection from root attrib
   - Track listing (name, type, index, color, group membership)
   - Tempo, time signature, markers, transport state
   - Dataclass models for all extracted data
   - JSON serialization

4. **Implement Tier 2 (Arrangement):**
   - MIDI clips: notes (pitch, start, duration, velocity), clip name, loop settings
   - Audio clips: file references, warp mode, warp markers
   - Clip slots and scenes
   - Arrangement timeline positions

5. **Implement Tier 3 (Mix):**
   - Volume, pan, sends per track
   - I/O routing (input/output type and channel)
   - Solo, mute, arm states

6. **Implement Tier 4 (Sound Design):**
   - Device chains per track
   - Plugin/instrument names and types (native vs VST vs AU vs Max4Live)
   - Device on/off state
   - Key parameter values
   - Rack detection (instrument rack, effect rack, drum rack) — at least identify them even if not fully traversing nested chains

7. **Implement Tier 5 (Detail) — stretch goal:**
   - Automation envelopes (parameter ID, breakpoints)
   - Clip envelopes
   - Groove pool settings
   - Follow actions
   - Freeze state

### Design constraints (from design-brief.md):

- Every field Optional[T] or sensible default — graceful degradation over crashes
- Flat convenience accessors, not deeply nested access patterns
- JSON-serializable dataclasses (suitable for stuffing into LLM context windows)
- Version detection from root.attrib['Creator'] before parsing
- Modular extractors so tiers can be loaded independently
- No external dependencies beyond Python stdlib

### Quality gates:

- Parser must not crash on malformed or unknown XML elements — skip and log warnings
- Include a __main__.py or CLI entry point: `python -m als_reader path/to/file.als` → prints JSON to stdout
- Write at least basic tests for Tier 1 parsing
- Include a brief README.md with usage examples

### Output location:

Build everything under /Users/brach/Documents/THE_FACTORY/enable/als-reader/

The docs/ folder already exists with research. Place source code in als_reader/ alongside it.
```

This prompt gives the agent everything: the research location, architectural decisions, build sequence, constraints, and quality gates. It should be able to work autonomously through all 5 tiers.
